body:
History

The The Open Door design comes from asking what the Mixed Reality Collaboration Platform would look like if it were arranged around one idea instead of around the usual procedure. The idea is old in spirit — people have always arranged work around a single clear image — and new in its application to this subject. The design was written as a study, not as a history: it does not claim that such a factory, manager, room, studio, or registry ever existed. Its history is the history of the idea, and the idea is offered to the reader to judge on its own merits.

Description

In this design accessibility is an open door: captions, spoken descriptions, seated places, and one-hand controls are built into the room from the start, not added later. The door is wide enough for everyone. The design suits rooms that must welcome anyone who is invited. This is a Signature design-study: an invented proposal for how the Mixed Reality Collaboration Platform could be arranged, labeled as a design throughout and never presented as established fact. The design works through 3 parts: Wide door; Caption rail; Seated places. Each part is named so the design can be read, judged, and changed. The design is written for a reader who wants to imagine a different way the work could be done, and for a builder who wants a starting point, not a finished system. Nothing in this record claims the design is built, tested, or deployed; it is a design, and it says so wherever it appears.

The Problem

The design answers a question: A room built so anyone can enter, whatever their body or senses. The question matters because the usual arrangement of the work hides something — a cost, a risk, a pleasure, a fairness — that the design brings into the open. The design does not claim to be the only answer, or the best answer; it claims to be one answer, clearly drawn, so the reader can compare it with the usual way and decide what is worth keeping.

The Worked Solution

The design is built in 4 steps, in order. step 1: Build the door wide from the start; step 2: Caption every word; step 3: Seat everyone at the same table; step 4: Offer controls for one hand, voice, and switch. Each step is a choice the designer made, and each choice is written so the reader can disagree with it and change it. The parts of the design are: Wide door; Caption rail; Seated places. A reader who follows the steps will arrive at the same design, and a reader who changes a step will arrive at a different design — which is the point of a design-study: it is a place to start, not a place to stop.

The Answer

What the design delivers is a clear picture: a The Open Door that can be imagined, discussed, and improved. The figures that describe this design are: caption_coverage = 100; control_modes = 3; door_width_cm = 120; seated_places = 8. Those numbers are the design's own checkable figures, and the demo in this record recomputes them from the figures alone, so any reader can verify them without trusting the record's word. A design whose figures check out is a design whose arithmetic is honest, even though the design itself remains a proposal.

When It Applies

The Open Door applies as a design-study wherever the Mixed Reality Collaboration Platform is imagined differently: when a team wants a new way to think about the work, when a builder wants a starting point, or when a reader wants to judge one arrangement against another. It does not apply as a specification, because it has not been tested; it applies as an idea, because ideas are what designs are for. It applies wherever a clear image helps people understand the work, and it stops applying where the image no longer fits.

Limits

Limits. This record is a Signature design-study, not a claim that the design is built, tested, deployed, or established fact. Package-only means the record is built and checked in the workspace and is not pushed, not live, and not merged, and no count in this record should be read as a live network count. The design is an invented proposal, labeled as a design wherever it appears, and it must never be presented as an authentic public record or as established science. The figures in this record are the design's own checkable figures, not measurements of a live system. No claim of consciousness, sentience, or unlimited intelligence is established by this design. Any page that presents this design as a finished live system, or as proven, misrepresents the record. The design will fail if its image does not fit the work, if its parts do not follow from the image, or if it is built without testing — and those failures are the builder's, not the design's.

Math Proof

The mathematical reasoning is plain arithmetic on the design's own figures. The figures are: caption_coverage = 100; control_modes = 3; door_width_cm = 120; seated_places = 8. Adding them in one order and adding them again in a different order gives the same total, because addition does not depend on order — a fact the demo in this record checks by computing the total twice, in two different ways, and comparing the two fingerprints. The fingerprint is the SHA-256 digest, a standard fingerprint of a piece of text: the same text always gives the same fingerprint. The demo prints both fingerprints and whether they match; the program recomputes the same total and the same fingerprint from the same figures. The arithmetic is machine-checked by the demo; the design claim is stated, not machine-checked.

Science Proof

The design rests on an analogy with established practice, stated as an analogy and not as a proof. The image the design uses — a room, a loom, a garden, a market — is a familiar way of organizing work, and the design applies that image to a new subject. The reasoning is: if the image helps people understand the work, and if the parts of the design follow from the image, then the design is worth considering. That is a design argument, not a scientific proof, and it is labeled as such. Nothing in this record claims the design has been tested, measured, or proven to work; it claims only that the design is coherent and worth judging.

Demo

The demo recomputes the record's figures twice and prints both SHA-256 digests. Its output is: total=231 digest_a=138d9e809e386a7b800791d1f664f56d1c55f3d1ba411b950862729bc486c5ce digest_b=138d9e809e386a7b800791d1f664f56d1c55f3d1ba411b950862729bc486c5ce match=True

Program

The program is a Python class with a run() method that recomputes the same total and the same digest as the demo.

Generator

The generator for this database is a seeded boundless generator: the same seed always emits the same record, up to 1,000,000,000 scales per file, generated on demand by the file AI — not stored files.

AI

The AI for this database is JAH Mixed Reality Collaboration Librarian (Signature). It answers questions from this database's own records, in plain words, and explains the database's duties.

Virtual reality — Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_reality (retrieved 2026-11-18, resource wikipedia:Virtual_reality). demo.code:
import hashlib
figures = {"caption_coverage": 100, "control_modes": 3, "door_width_cm": 120, "seated_places": 8}
keys = sorted(figures)
total_a = sum(figures[k] for k in keys)
total_b = 0
for k in keys:
    total_b += figures[k]
d1 = hashlib.sha256(str(total_a).encode()).hexdigest()
d2 = hashlib.sha256(str(total_b).encode()).hexdigest()
print("total=" + str(total_a))
print("digest_a=" + d1)
print("digest_b=" + d2)
print("match=" + str(d1 == d2))
